          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. On 24.07.2026, we took notice of the status reports filed by
the Central Bureau of Investigation, the SITs, as well as Mr.
Dattatray  Padsalgikar,  former  Director  General  of  Police,
Maharashtra, who has been appointed by this Court to monitor the
ongoing investigation, and upon consideration thereof:
(i) The  State  of  Manipur  was  directed  to  provide  full
cooperation to the investigating agencies to overcome the
difficulties highlighted in the status report;
(ii) The applicants raising grievances regarding some missing
persons were directed to approach the Hon’ble Chief Justice of
the High Court of Manipur, so that those matters could also be
entrusted for investigation to one of the SITs;
(iii) The petitioners were permitted to approach the three-
Judge Committee headed by Justice Gita Mittal, former Chief
Justice of Jammu and Kashmir High Court, regarding dispute
over one of the sites, where a lawful structure was in
existence but had been demolished; and
(iv) The  legal  aid  counsel  were  directed  to  immediately
coordinate with the offices of Hon’ble the Chief Justices of
the High Courts of Manipur and Guwahati for obtaining the
copies of the chargesheets.
7

## Page 222

2. In  deference  thereto,  the  Manipur  State  Legal  Services
Authority has filed a status report dated 07.08.2026. Paragraphs 4,
5, and 6 thereof read as follows:
“4. It is respectfully submitted that a total of 31
(thirty-one) cases involving heinous crimes were entrusted
to  the  Central  Bureau  of  Investigation  (CBI)  for
investigation.  Of  these,  05  (five)  cases  pertain  to
incidents of arms looting and therefore do not involve any
victims. The remaining 26 cases involve victims and the
MASLSA has appointed Legal Aid Counsel for each victim in
all such cases.
5. That, as per the reports received from the concerned
DLSAs, copies of chargesheets have been furnished to all
victims/victim’s family members through concerned Legal
Aid Counsel in all the 18 (eighteen) charge-sheeted cases.
Acknowledgments/receipts confirming receipt of the charge-
sheets have also been obtained from all the concerned
victims’ victim’s family members and their Legal Aid
Counsel.
A detailed statement presented as a tabulation
containing the particulars of all the 18 charge-
sheeted  cases,  along  with  copies  of  the
acknowledgments/receipts are enclosed at Annexure-
IV.
6. That, it is respectfully submitted that the matter is
being regularly monitored by Hon’ble Chief Justice, High
Court of Manipur and Hon’ble Executive Chairman, Manipur
State Legal Services Authority and directions issued by
the Hon’ble Supreme Court have been duly complied.”
 
3. At this stage, Ms. Vrinda Grover, learned counsel for some of
the petitioners, has pointed out that the Sessions Case number and
other relevant particulars of 18 cases, where chargesheets have
been filed, ought to be brought on record as it will enable the
Legal Aid Counsel as well as victims/their families to have access
to the records and facilitate the trial. We accept this suggestion
and direct Manipur State Legal Services Authority to obtain the
full particulars of the Sessions Trial number, etc., from the
courts concerned and place them on record in a tabulated form.
8

## Page 223

4. The learned Additional Solicitor General of India has also
handed over a status report submitted by the CBI and NIA. In the
status report on behalf of CBI, it is, inter alia, pointed out that
chargesheets have been filed in 27 cases before the Special Judge,
CBI & NIA, Guwahati, which includes 5 closure reports. In addition,
4 cases are still under investigation. There are said to be a total
of 904 witnesses, out of which only 5 witnesses in 2 cases have
been examined. The remaining 899 witnesses are yet to be examined.
The status of trial of CBI cases has also been placed on record in
a tabulated form. Having regard to the total number of witnesses
proposed to be examined and the voluminous evidence, we request the
Chief Justice of Gauhati High Court to consider the feasibility of
allowing the CBI/NIA Court to exclusively deal with Manipur-related
CBI/NIA cases, and let other cases, which were entrusted to the
Presiding Officer, be transferred to some other Court. Similarly,
the Hon’ble Chief Justice, in consultation with other concerned
authorities, may also consider the desirability of constituting two
exclusive special courts, i.e., one for CBI cases and another for
NIA cases. It would be appreciated if the Registrar General of the
High Court submits a status report in this regard before the next
date of hearing. 
5. The NIA, in its status report, has pointed out that a total of
thirty cases relating to Manipur violence are pending, out of which
charge-sheets have been filed in 15 cases, while investigation is
still underway in the remaining 15 cases. These cases involve 47
accused persons. Trial has commenced in 6 cases. The details of the
9

## Page 224

15 cases, where chargesheets have been filed have also been
appended along with this status report.

Maharashtra,  who  has  been  appointed  to  oversee  the  ongoing
investigation in the Manipur violence cases, has also filed a
status report dated 03.08.2026, inter alia, explaining that in July
2026, several arson incidents and road blockades by some community
groups were reported. Armed attacks on the CRPF CoBRA Unit near
Bitiang village, Noney district were also noted. There were also
other incidents, including attacks on the Assam Rifles, use of an
IED blast for causing damage to public infrastructure, and the
recent public protest demanding the State Government to update the
NRC before conducting the census in the State. It is pointed out
that the joint efforts of the Manipur Police and the Central
Security  Forces  have  been  successful  in  recovering  arms  and
ammunition as well as arresting the anti-social elements involved
in such disruptive and destructive activites.
7. We trust and hope that irrespective of the sensitive law-and-
order situation, the SITs, CBI, and NIA shall continue with their
ongoing investigation uninterruptedly, and the State Government
will ensure full cooperation and assistance to the Central Agencies
and  SITs  in  taking  the  pending  investigation  to  a  logical
conclusion. The investigative agencies, the State Legal Services
Authority, as well as the State Authorities shall file their
respective status reports before the next date of hearing.

been specifically mentioned, along with the Government of India’s
PMAY-G scheme, providing Rs.5 lakh for Kutcha house, Rs.7 lakh for
Semi-pucca  house,  and  Rs.10  lakh  for  Pucca  house.  It  was
highlighted that 12,000 houses for affected families have been
approved so far under the PMAY-G scheme. It was also highlighted
that 3000 temporary shelters have been constructed by the State

is being provided, in installments, for fully burnt houses, besides
Rs.75,000 per household for partially damaged houses.

O R D E R
CIVIL APPEAL NO.2712/2020
1. The present appeal has been filed assailing the
impugned judgement dated 13.01.2020 passed by National
Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (for short,
‘the National Commission’), wherein, the appeal filed
by appellant/Opposite Party No. 3 – Mitsubishi Motors
Corporation, has been dismissed by affirming the order
dated 13.12.2018 passed by the Delhi State Consumer
Disputes Redressal Commission (for short, ‘the State
Commission).
2. The brief facts leading up to the filing of
present  appeals  are  that  the  respondent  No.1/
Complainant  had  purchased  a  vehicle  namely,
“Mitsubishi Outlander” from the Authorized Dealer/

## Page 228

2
Opposite Party No. 1. On 20.03.2016, the vehicle was
hit by a flying stone, due to which the windshield of
the vehicle was cracked. Subsequently, the vehicle was
sent  to  the  Authorized  Dealer  for  carrying  out
repairs, however, while taking back the delivery from
them, the complainant had noticed loud noises coming
from  the  vehicle  on  23.03.2016.  The  complainant
neither took the delivery of the vehicle nor settled
the bill for repairs. 
3. Thereafter, on 24.03.2016, the Complainant was
informed that the noise in the vehicle could be due
to the Continuously Variable Transmission (for short,
‘CVT’), for which the CVT fluid was to be replaced.
As the fluid was not available in Delhi, it was
requisitioned from Chennai, but the stock received
was allegedly contaminated. After a period of three
weeks,  the  fluid  was  replaced  and  trials  were
conducted,  however,  the  noise  from  the  vehicle
persisted. The Authorized Dealer and Hindustan Motors
Ltd./Opposite Party No. 2, had suggested that the
problem could be with the gear box. On 04.05.2016,
the Complainant was informed that contaminated fluid
was  found  inside  the  CVT  Unit.  The  Complainant
contended that since the CVT Unit was a sealed unit,
such contamination was not possible, alleging that

## Page 229

3
there  is  a  manufacturing/inherent  defect  in  the
vehicle. 
4. Despite repeated attempts, the Opposite Parties
could not identify the cause of the noise. As the
vehicle remained unusable, the Complainant sought a
definite timeline for its repair and, on 16.06.2016,
he raised a debit note of Rs. 25,87,207/- towards the
amount  spent  on  the  vehicle.  On  18.06.2016,  the
Authorized Dealer informed him that the valve body
and reverse clutch parts had been replaced, but the
noise persisted and the entire CVT Unit would now
have  to  be  changed,  at  the  expense  of  the
Complainant, since the vehicle was out of warranty. 
5. Alleging that the sale of Mitsubishi Outlander
Car had been discontinued in India, due to several
complaints, the Complainant alleged restrictive and
unfair trade practices and deficiency in service on
the  part of  the Opposite  Parties and  filed the
Consumer Complaint No. 709/2016 before the State
Commission.  Vide the said complaint, he prayed for
refund  of  value  of  the  vehicle,  amounts  towards
interest, registration charges along with an interest
of 24%, as well as compensation against mental trauma
and  agony,  expenditure  for  alternative  mode  of
transportation and litigation expenses.

## Page 230

4
6. The  State  Commission  vide judgement  dated
13.12.2018,  partly  allowed  the  complaint  while
directing the Opposite Parties No. 1,2,3 and 5, i.e.,
Asian  Motors,  Hindustan  Motors  Ltd.,  Mitsubishi
Motors and Hindustan Motor Finance Corporation Ltd.
to refund a sum of Rs. 10,12,500/-, being 50% of the
value of the vehicle, as well as directed to pay the
compensation to the effect of Rs. 1,00,000/- for
mental agony and trauma and Rs. 50,000/- against
actual  expenditure  for  alternative  mode  of
transportation to the complainant. Aggrieved, the
appellant preferred an appeal before the National
Commission.
7. The National Commission affirmed the judgement
dated 13.12.2018, and dismissed the appeals by noting
that the Opposite Parties could not find the exact
cause  of  noise  generated  by  the  vehicle  between
24.03.2016 and 04.05.2016. There was a deficiency in
service by not changing the CVT fluid at the time of
4th service of the vehicle on 21.05.2014 .  It was
observed  that  the  vehicle  was  equipped  with  a
computer system which would warn of any malfunction,
thus, if the CVT fluid had been contaminated before
23.03.2016, a warning should have appeared on the
display panel. Further, despite the involvement of

## Page 231

5
technical staff from Chennai, the Opposite Parties
failed to identify the exact cause of the noise for a
considerable  period  and  kept  replacing  different
parts without resolving the problem, which indicated
a major manufacturing defect in the vehicle. It was
further noted that Fuel Pump Assembly was replaced by
the  Authorized  Dealer,  free  of  cost,  which  was
indicative of an inherent defect in the vehicle.
Lastly,  the  complainant  had  discovered  several
complaints regarding problems in different parts of
the same vehicle, including the CVT, for which the
vehicle  had  allegedly  been  recalled  by  the
Manufacturer. It was held that the State Commission
had rightly awarded a refund of 50% of the value of
the  vehicle  along  with  the  other  compensation
amounts. Aggrieved, the appellant is before this
Court.
8. We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing for the appellant and the respondent No.1,
who appears in-person.
9. We have also perused the decisions rendered by
the State Commission and the National Commission. 
10. Insofar as the appellant - Mitsubishi Motors
Corporation  is  concerned,  we  find  force  in  the
submission  made  by  the  learned  Senior  counsel

## Page 232

6
appearing for the appellant that the appellant was not
involved in the manufacturing of the subject vehicle
and the same was manufactured by Hindustan Motors
Ltd./Pro-forma respondent No. 3/Opposite Party No. 2,
pursuant to the execution of the License Agreement
dated  21.03.2008  and  the  Component  Supply  and
Distribution Agreement dated 04.05.2010 between them.
Therefore, since the concerned part of the subject
vehicle has not been manufactured by the appellant,
the question of fixing liability upon it, would not
arise.
11. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to
set aside the decisions rendered by both the State
Commission and the National Commission, insofar as the
present appellant - Mitsubishi Motors Corporation is
concerned.
12. Accordingly,  the  impugned  judgement  dated
13.01.2020 passed by the National Consumer Disputes
Redressal  Commission  stands  set  aside  qua the
appellant - Mitsubishi Motors Corporation.
13. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

## Page 233

7
CIVIL APPEAL NO.367/2023
15. The facts in the both the appeals are same, and
do not require repetition. Insofar as the appeal filed
by  the  appellant  –  M/S.  Hindustan  Motor  Finance
Corporation Ltd. is concerned, both the forums have
considered the issue pertaining to the warranty of the
vehicle not being brought up for inspection at an
earlier point of time. The said finding is borne out
of the facts.
16. We  are  not  inclined  to  interfere  with  the
impugned order passed by the National Commission,
especially, with respect to specific findings given on
the oil/fluid in the CVT Unit, which was found to be
contaminated. 
17. Though we are in agreement with the learned
counsel appearing for the appellant with respect to
the  submission  made  on  the  manufacturing  defect,
considering that both the forums have found deficiency
in service on the other aspects, we are inclined to
confirm  the  decision  rendered  in  the  impugned
judgement dated 13.01.2020 qua the appellant.
18. The order passed by the National Commission,
affirming the decision of the State Commission will
have to be complied within a period of three months
from the date of receipt of a copy of this order. 

## Page 234

8
19. As  we  find  no  perversity  in  the  decision
rendered  qua the  appellant,  the  appeal  stands
dismissed.
20. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

                            O R D E R
Heard Mr. S.V. Raju, learned ASG, Mr. Pitambar Acharya,

## Page 244

learned Advocate General for the State of Odisha, and Mr. Siddharth
Dave, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the Allahabad High
Court. 
2. Pursuant to our earlier directions, Mr. S.V. Raju, learned ASG
has placed a tabular chart setting out the stand taken by the
various States in the matter and has also placed his suggestions
before us. He has taken us through the same issue-wise. We record
our appreciation for the exercise undertaken and also place on
record the efforts of Mr. Hitartha Raja and Mr. Aryansh Shukla in
assisting Mr. S.V. Raju, learned ASG.
3. We find that the suggestions put forth are practical and may
be implemented as a starting point. However, for working out the
actual modalities for implementation of the said suggestions, we
request Mr. S.V. Raju, learned ASG to convene a meeting of all the
Registrar Generals of the High Courts, the Directors General of
Police, the Heads of the Departments of Prisons of the respective
States  and  the  senior-most  Secretary  of  the  Department  of
Information  Technology  of  the  respective  States,  the  learned
Advocate Generals, the Law Secretaries and the senior-most officer
of the Home Department of the respective States. 
4. A meeting shall accordingly be convened. Preferably, the
aforesaid officers shall attend the meeting in person. If, for any
compelling reason, any of them is unable to do so, he or she may
join  the  meeting  through  virtual  mode.  However,  under  no
circumstances, shall any of the officers named above be exempted
from attending the meeting, either physically or virtually. They
shall also not be permitted to delegate the responsibility to any
junior officer. We further direct that where any Officer is unable

## Page 245

to attend the meeting physically for any compelling reason, the
concerned officers may join through video conferencing, with the
caveat that each State shall log into the video conference through
a single device, so that all the concerned Officers are present
together at one place while participating in the proceedings
virtually.
5. The aforesaid exercise shall be completed within six weeks. To
facilitate the process, we request Mr. S.V. Raju, learned ASG to
circulate his suggestions to the States as well as the High Courts
through their learned counsel appearing in the present proceedings.
The same be done within one week. The concerned officers shall
thereafter be prepared on the issues flagged and the suggestions
made by Mr. S.V. Raju, learned ASG, and the conference shall be
held within the next four weeks. Mr. S.V. Raju, learned ASG, is
requested to prepare a final common Standard Operating Procedure in
the matter. We indicate that initially, an endeavour should be made
to put the suggested practice into operation. A time frame may also
be indicated by each State for implementing and putting in place
the infrastructure required for the said purpose.
6. The  High  Courts  may  also  appraise  the  situation,  as
implementation of the aforesaid mechanism may require special
deputation of Judicial Officers to various prisons.
7. A suggestion has been made that whenever a Judicial Officer is
deputed to a prison on any particular day, he or she may be made
in-charge of the cases on that day in which the attendance of the
accused is required.
8. The aforesaid modality may be worked out in consultation with
the concerned State Authorities.

## Page 246

9. Mr. Y.B. Khurania, the Director General of Police, Odisha, is
present.
10. Having considered the matter, we are satisfied with the steps
taken by him. Accordingly, his personal appearance stands dispensed
with.
11. All affidavits filed by the States and the High Courts till
today are taken on record and accepted.
12. As prayed for, the matter be listed on 29.09.2026 at 2:00 p.m.

## Page 248

2. The present Contempt Petition has been filed alleging
contempt of the order of this Court dated 03.02.2026 passed
in SLP(Civil) No. 27640 of 2025. The relevant directions in
the aforesaid order read as under:
“Heard learned counsels for the parties. 
2. The issue which is crystallized before us is
whether  the  possession  of  portion  of  the
area/land in dispute, which is presently with
the petitioner and of which the respondent No.1
claims to be landlord (original leaseholder) is
a public road.
3. Having gone through the material on record,
we find that basically the issue of whether a
road existed prior to the creation of tenancy,
either  in  favour  of  the  petitioner  or
respondent No.1, is a matter of fact to be
decided with reference to the contemporaneous
revenue records maintained by the State.
4. The said exercise be done by the State
Authorities within two weeks from today. Upon
demarcation being made, the State Authorities
shall ensure that the entire road along with
the  pavement  etc.  as  is  reflected  in  the
contemporaneous revenue records, is made free
of encroachment and restored in the shape of a
road accessible to the public at large without
any hindrance from any party concerned.
5. With regard to any other dispute, relating
to any other land beyond what is shown as a
road, the same is left open to be decided
inter-se between the parties in appropriately
constituted proceedings before the appropriate
forum in accordance with law.
2

## Page 249

6. The petition stands disposed of in the
aforesaid terms.
7. It is further made clear that the order
impugned will not come in the way of any of the
parties to assert their right(s) for being
given lease of any portion of land or for being
suitably rehabilitated at any other place. If
such a representation is made by the party
concerned before the Competent Authority, the
same  shall  be  looked  into  and  appropriate
decision  be  taken  in  accordance  with  law
without being prejudiced by the present order
or the order impugned.
8. The work of actual demarcation would be
carried out on 10 th of February 2026 at 11:00
a.m. at the actual site. No separate notice is
required to be given to the parties, as all of
them are present before this Court. Even if any
of the parties do not appear, the exercise
shall continue till it is taken to its logical
conclusion  by  the  Authorities  concerned.
Thereafter, the entire road along with its
pavement  would  be  made  free  from  any
encroachment.
9.  After  the  order  was  dictated,  learned
counsel for the petitioner submitted that one
of the issues raised by him before the High
Court was that Section 10 of the Uttar Pradesh
Regulation of Urban Premises Tenancy Act, 2021
was ultra vires in as much as, it did not give
any right to the tenant to contest a petition
by the landlord for enhancement of rent, which
has not been decided by the High Court and on
this aspect, as this Court is also not going
3

## Page 250

into the issue, he may be permitted to move
before the High Court in a fresh proceeding
limited to the challenge to the vires of such
provision  and  consequential  orders  based
thereupon.
10.  We  find  the  prayer  to  be  reasonable.
Accordingly, liberty is given to the petitioner
to move the High Court for going into the above
aspect. We further clarify that we have not
expressed any opinion on the merits of such
challenge, if made before the High Court.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also
stand disposed of.”
3. Pursuant to the said order, site inspection was done
by  the  authorities  in  the  presence  of  the  parties
concerned and based on the same, encroachments from the
road as well as from the covered pathways were removed as
per the stand of Agra Development Authority. In the
affidavit filed on behalf of respondents no. 2 and 7 (Agra
Municipal Corporation), it transpires that there is a
straight  road  and  there  are  covered  pavements  also
abutting the road on both sides.
4. From  the  photographs  brought  on  record  in  the
application seeking directions (IA No.136073/2026) filed
on behalf of the proposed intervenor-Pradeep Kumar Jain,
it transpires that the width of the road is 30 feet and
covered pavement on each side is 8 feet wide. In the note
handed over by the learned Attorney General, it is stated
4

## Page 251

that at the time of grant of lease by the Municipal
Authority on 14.05.1947, the width of the road was shown
as 30 feet at one end, and at the other end it was 29 feet
with covered footpaths of 8 feet on each side. In the
exercise  undertaken  pursuant  to  our  order  dated
03.02.2026,  the  same  has  been  restored  free  of
encroachment.
5. The District Administration Agra has also filed its
counter affidavit, in which, the stand taken is that the
road  and  the  pavements  have  been  cleared  of  all
encroachments. However, with regard to grant of lease
itself, proceedings have been initiated and will be taken
to their logical conclusion without delay.
6. Mr. P.S. Patwalia, learned Senior Counsel for the
petitioner submitted that till date the encroachment is
there in the sense that even the Committee which was
constituted to do the fact finding has found that there is
encroachment, which remains till date and some of the
encroachment is on Nazul Land. It was further contended
that the so called landlord while making construction has
encroached upon both the Nazul land and the road, and the
construction is required to be demolished in terms of the
order dated 03.02.2026.
7. Having considered the matter holistically in its
entirety, we are clear that the Court is required to
consider only the aspect as to whether there has been
5

## Page 252

contempt of the order dated 03.02.2026.
8. As would be clear from the order which has been
quoted above, the direction was clear and specific. The
demarcation had to be made by the State Authorities with
regard  to  the  road  and  pavements  as  reflected  in
contemporaneous revenue record and then making them free
of encroachment. In view of the categorical stand taken by
the official respondents, that at the time of grant of the
lease by the Municipal Authority, i.e., on 14.05.1947
there was a 30 feet road and 8 feet footpath on each side,
which was covered, and the same being reflected from the
photographs and now being made free of encroachment, we
find that there is no contempt as of today and if there
had been any violation earlier, today, the same stands
purged.
9. Accordingly, the Contempt Petition stands dismissed.
10. However, we are equally concerned with regard to the
findings which have come through inspection. As we have
been told by Mr. S.D. Sanjay, learned Senior Advocate for
District  Administration  Agra  as  also  by  Mr.  R.
Venkataramani,  learned  Attorney  General  for  the  Agra
Municipal Corporation, the authorities are directed to
take matters to their logical conclusion in accordance
with law expeditiously.
11. Before parting, we may indicate that in the earlier
order dated 22.05.2026, we had also directed that all up-
6

## Page 253

to-date  payment  of  rent  should  be  cleared  by  the
petitioner and the same admittedly has not been done.
Though we could have  suo  moto  initiated contempt for
violation of that part of the order, however, we are
refraining from doing so, as we are finally closing the
proceedings. 
12. Pending applications, including the applications for
intervention/impleadment, shall also stand disposed of.

    IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
 CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.________ OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(Criminal) No.18879/2025)
SATISH DIXIT                                       Appellant(s)
                             VERSUS
THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ANR.                  Respondent(s)
     O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant has called in question
the order passed by the High Court declining to
quash the charge-sheet and the cognizance order
passed by the learned Special Judge (SC/ST
Act), Auraiya in connection with FIR No.1144 of
2022 registered with Police Station Auraiya,
District Auraiya for offences punishable under
Sections 147, 419, 420, 467, 468, 471, 394,
511, 504, 506  of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
and Section 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and
the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities)
Act, 1989.
3. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant
submits that the appellant was lending money to
the respondent no.2, Pappu Valmiki, at regular
intervals and, at one point in time, respondent

## Page 267

2
no.2 owed a total sum of Rs.6,00,000/- to the
appellant.  In  repayment  of  the  said  loan
amount, the respondent no.2 issued a cheque of
Rs.6,00,000/- in favour of the appellant, which
was dishonoured when the same was presented for
encashment.  This  led  to  the  filing  of  a
complaint  against  respondent  no.2  for  an
offence punishable under Section 138 of the
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (for short,
the ‘NI Act’).
4. Subsequently,  the  respondent  no.2
paid the amount of Rs.7,55,000/- through Bank
Draft No. 00177 issued by the Central Bank of
India, Khanpur Branch, Auriya and a compromise
was entered between the parties on 17.12.2025
which has been accepted by the concerned Court.
A copy of the compromise is placed on record by
way  of  an  application  bearing  I.A.
No.224573/2026  seeking  permission  to  file
additional documents.
5. In  the  present  matter,  the
respondent no.2 lodged an FIR on 26.12.2022
alleging that, from the year 2015 onwards till
10.08.2022,  the  appellant  had  fraudulently
withdrawn a total sum of Rs.40,00,000/- from

## Page 268

3
his  account  and  had  threatened,  criminally
intimidated and used foul language with caste-
related slurs.
6. We have perused the FIR and other
related papers in the charge-sheet, including
the  statement  of  the  complainant's  wife
recorded under Section 161 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973, in which she stated
that her husband had taken loans on interest
from the present appellant many times and that
the appellant was doing business of lending
money on interest.  She also stated that, if
the  money  was  not  returned  on  time,  the
appellant would get signatures made on cheques
and keep their ATM cards with him. 
7. Respondent no.2 has filed copies of
his bank statement of account in an application
bearing I.A. No. 224443 of 2026, which is an
application  seeking  permission  to  file
additional  documents,  a  perusal  of  which
demonstrate that from the year 2015 onwards,
respondent no.2 has been issuing cheques of
different amounts ranging from Rs.10,000/- to
Rs.1,00,000/- at regular intervals. The total
payment made to the appellant during all these

## Page 269

4
years would come to Rs.2,71,700/-. Similarly,
some payments have also been made in the name
of Maa Pitambra Mobile from April, 2021 onwards
amounting to Rs.1,27,614/-.
8. On perusal of the Bank statement of
account of respondent no.2, it clearly reflects
that the respondent no.2 owed money to the
appellant,  which  has  been  repaid  through
cheques and UPI payments. Thus, the whole story
mentioned in the FIR that the appellant had
fraudulently withdrawn Rs.40,00,000/- is not at
all  reflected  from  the  bank  statement  of
account of respondent no.2. Moreover, if the
fraud was to such an extent covering huge
amount of Rs.40,00,000/-, it was surprising as
to why the respondent No.2 kept silent for
about 07 years before lodging the FIR in the
year 2022.
9. It is all the more surprising that,
if the respondent no.2 had been defrauded of a
sum of Rs.40,00,000/- during the period from
2015 to 2022, in respect of which an FIR was
lodged on 26.12.2022, why did respondent no.2
agree to make a payment of Rs.7,55,000/- to the
appellant on 17.12.2025, i.e., nearly three

## Page 270

5
years after lodging the FIR.
10. Considering the above broad features
of the case, we are of the considered view that
the  allegations  made  in  the  FIR  and  the
ingredients  thereof  appear  to  be  highly
improbable, particularly in the light of the
compromise entered into between the parties in
the  proceedings  initiated  by  the  present
appellant  against  respondent  no.2  for  the
offence punishable under Section 138 of the NI
Act.  Allowing  the  trial  to  continue  would
amount  to  subjecting  the  appellant  to  the
trauma of a trial in which there is no evidence
of fraudulent withdrawal of Rs.40,00,000/- from
his account.
11. At this stage, learned counsel for
the appellant would submit that the respondent
no.2 did not compromise in the present case,
fearing withdrawal of an amount of Rs.75,000/-,
granted to him by the State Government under a
welfare  scheme,  wherein,  in  case  a  member
belonging SC/ ST category is cheated, the State
Government offers compensation.
12. Without  commenting  on  the  above
aspect of the matter, we deem it appropriate to

## Page 271

6
quash FIR No.1144 of 2022, registered with
Police  Station  Auraiya,  District  Auraiya,
against  the  appellant  and  all  subsequent
proceedings, including the charge-sheet, the
cognizance order and the criminal proceedings
arising therefrom.
13. The appeal stands disposed of in the
aforesaid terms.
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,
shall also stand disposed of.

2. The present appeal arises from the final judgment 
and order dated 02.09.2025 passed by the High Court of 
Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 

## Page 283

2 
 
4068 of 2024, which had partly enhanced the 
compensation awarded to the appellant for injuries 
sustained in a motor vehicle accident on 27.11.2020. 
3. The brief facts are that on 27.11.2020, the 
appellant, then aged 28 years and working as a 
labourer, met with a motor vehicle accident involving 
a Hyva Truck (Registration No. MP66D0802). The 
appellant sustained grievous injuries to both legs, 
leading to the amputation of his right leg above the 
knee and the surgical insertion of a rod in his left 
leg. The medical board certified a 90% permanent 
disability; however, the appellant contends that as an 
uneducated labourer, he has suffered 100% functional 
disability as he is now incapable of performing any 
manual labor. 
4. The proceedings originated before the IVth 
Additional Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT), 
Singrauli (M.P.) in Claim Case No. 25/2021. Vide award 
dated 24.02.2024, the Tribunal partly allowed the 
claim, awarding a total compensation of Rs. 29,59,108/- 
with 7% interest. The Tribunal assessed the appellant's 

## Page 284

3 
 
monthly income at Rs. 12,000/- based on daily wages of 
Rs. 400/-, applied a multiplier of 16 (considering his 
age as 32 years), and calculated 90% permanent 
disability.  
5. Aggrieved by the inadequate compensation and the 
lack of future prospects, the appellant preferred 
Miscellaneous Appeal No. 4068 of 2024 before the High 
Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur. The High Court, 
vide its order dated 02.09.2025, enhanced the total 
compensation to Rs. 47,09,108/ -, representing an 
increase of Rs. 17,50,000/- over the Tribunal's award.  
6. Regarding the assessment of income, we find that 
the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal and the High Court 
erroneously fixed the appellant's monthly income at Rs. 
12,000/- based on a restrictive calculation of minimum 
daily wages at Rs. 400/ -. However, a perus al of the 
record reveals that the appellant, in his deposition 
as PW -1, categorically stated he was earning Rs. 
20,000/- per month. This testimony is substantially 
corroborated by Sh. Vinay Kumar Paul, the Deputy 
General Manager of Respondent No. 1 (the employer), who 

## Page 285

4 
 
admitted in his deposition that the appellant's fixed 
salary was approximately Rs. 15,000/ - per month. 
Furthermore, the appellant provided a detailed 
breakdown of the remaining Rs. 5,000/- per month, which 
he earned through Overtime, Night Allowance, and a  
Special Allowance specifically designated for the 
hazardous nature of his work in coal mines. Considering 
these actual emoluments and the employer's own 
admissions, which were overlooked by the courts below, 
we find it just and proper to increase and fix the 
assessed monthly income at Rs. 20,000/- 
7. Upon hearing the learned counsel for both parties 
and perusing the record, given the severity of the 
injuries, we find that the compensation further 
requires re -computation under conventional heads  to 
meet the standard of "just compensation": 
8. Based on the aforementioned findings, the final 
compensation is re-calculated as follows:

 O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Our Order dated 11th August, 2026 reads thus:
“1. Having heard the learned senior counsel appearing for the
parties and having gone through the materials on record, we are
of the view that the presence of the Respondent No.6 - Kolkata
Municipal  Corporation,  the  respondent  no.7-  Municipal
Commissioner, Kolkata Municipal Commission and the respondent
no.8-Director  General,  Kolkata  Municipal  Corporation,
respectively, and other respondents is very much required.
2. We would like to know what is the stance of the Corporation
as regards the prima facie finding recorded by the High court in
its impugned interim order that the land on which construction
has come up is a water body classified as “Danga” or “Pukur”.
3. We want a comprehensive report in this regard by the next
date of hearing. We are conscious of the fact that what is
impugned before us is an interim order(s) and the main matter is
coming up for hearing on 28.8.2026 before the High Court.
However, we would like to know the stance of the Corporation.
4. Issue notice, returnable on 17.08.2026.

## Page 291

2
5. In the meantime, the impugned interim order(s) passed by the
High Court shall remain stayed from its operation.
6. Dasti service, in addition, is permitted.
7. No further time will be granted to any of the respondents
on returnable date.”
3. In pursuance of our Order, referred to above, the Respondent
Nos.6, 7, and 8 respectively have filed an affidavit duly  affirmed
by Director General (Building), Kolkata Municipal Corporation.
4. What we have been able to gather from the counter filed by the
Corporation is that on 9th December 2019, the Government of West
Bengal, Office of District Land and Land Reforms, issued a land
conversion certificate under Section 4C of the West Bengal Land
Reforms Act, wherein the three plot numbers, being 717, 719/1176,
and 720 respectively, were allowed conversion for the purpose of
multi-storied housing. 
5. In para 9 of the counter filed by the Corporation, the
following has been stated:
“A. Under relevant Land Reforms law the State Government is
competent  to  grant  any  change  of  user;
B. It is submitted that under Rule 166 of Land and Land Reforms
Manual  1991,  allowed  conversion  before  making  appropriate
application and the cut off date in this regard was 24.03.1986;
C. According to Inspection Book of Corporation in relation to
page  corresponding  1983-84  the  property  was  factory;
D. Hence, the property though not formally converted before
2017-19 actually stood converted in its use from 1983-84 and
thus, the Conversion certificates issued in 2017-19 do not run
counter to the same;
E. All plots were granted conversion in accordance with Section
4C of Land Reforms Act 1955 and Corporation acted within its
power to sanction plan for the project.
 

## Page 292

3
6. We heard Mr. Mukul Rohatgi and Mr. Nakul Dewan, the learned
Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant and on the other hand,
Mr. Kunal Chatterjee, the learned counsel appearing for the Corpo -
ration, Mr. Gopal Sankaranarayanan, the learned Senior counsel and
Mr. Biswaroop Bhattacharya , the learned counsel appearing for the
original writ petitioner(s) and Mr. Uddyam Mukherjee, the learned
counsel  appearing  for  the  State  of  West  Bengal.
7. Mr.  Gopal  Sankaranarayanan,  the  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing  for  the  original  writ  petitioners,  has  manifold
contentions to raise as regards the stance of the Corporation which
has been placed before us today by way of an affidavit. 
8. We are of the view that since the matter is at large before
the High Court, we should not express any opinion on the merits of
any  of  the  issues  arising  in  this  particular  litigation.
9. All that we want to say is that, having regard to the specific
stance of the Corporation as on date before us, we would not
approve the grant of interim relief by the High Court restraining
the  appellant  from  proceeding  further  with  the  development/
construction. Accordingly, the impugned Order passed by the High
Court to the extent it has granted interim relief stands set aside.
10. We leave it to the High Court to decide all issues between the
parties. 
11. It shall be open for the learned counsel appearing for the
parties to raise all  contentions available to them in law.
12. In the peculiar facts of this case, and more particularly
keeping in mind that third-party rights have also been created, it
will be in fitness of things if the High Court gives some priority

## Page 293

4
to the main matter and decides it once and for all, finally.  
13. With the aforesaid, the appeals stand disposed of.
14. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

from today.  The said amount shall be paid in equal monthly
installments.  The transaction would not adversely affect
the rights of the respondent-bank reserving its share(s).

amicable settlement between both the parties. As per the
said compromise, the disputed land has been divided equally
between both the parties. Party No.2 shall execute and get
registered the Sale Deed in favour of Party No.1 in respect of
one-half share of the disputed land. Thereafter, after proper
measurement, the land shall be divided equally between
both the parties at the spot. Both the parties shall be bound
to  submit  this  written  compromise  before  the  Hon’ble
Supreme Court in accordance with the procedure prescribed
by law. Thereafter, neither party shall have any objection or
claim against the other. The trees standing on the land shall
also be divided equally. The Government watercourse (Khal)
shall subsequently be laid through the middle of the said 16
Marlas, and thereafter the land of both the parties shall be
carved out equally. The responsibility for withdrawal of the
case and for getting the stay order vacated shall be that of
Party  No.1.  If  either  party  resiles  from  this  written
compromise, the defaulting party shall be liable to pay a
sum of  ₹10,00,000/- (Rupees Ten Lakhs only)  to the
other party as compensation. Therefore, being in our full
senses and of our own free will, without any pressure or
coercion, we have executed this Compromise Deed in the
presence of the witnesses on  25.07.2022, so that it may
serve as evidence whenever required.

Sections 3 and 10 of the Rajasthan Public

State of Rajasthan, we are informed that the
charges have already been framed and the trial
has commenced, wherein 4 out of the 22 listed
witnesses have been examined.  
4. As  there  is  no  possibility  of  the  trial
concluding any time soon in the near future,

the trial and shall not delay the proceedings
therein.

application for setting aside abatement is condoned,
application for substitution and setting aside the
abatement are allowed. 
4. This appeal is filed against the impugned order
dated  07.04.2022  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Judicature at Bombay in Writ Petition No. 6159 of
2011.
5. The appellant before us is an Auction Purchaser
and has challenged the impugned order, by which the
High Court has affirmed the decision of the Debts
Recovery Appellate Tribunal [DRAT] dated 27.06.2011,
reversing the order passed by the Debts Recovery
Tribunal [DRT] dated 26.03.2008.  By the said order,
the DRT dismissed the appeal filed by the respondents

## Page 391

2
– debtors against the auction sale dated 29.12.2003,
as affirmed on 24.05.2004.
6. We need not dwell into the detailed facts of the
case for the reason that various submissions raised by
Mr. Parag Tripathi, learned senior counsel appearing
for the Auction Purchaser have not been dealt with in
detail by the High Court. This is perhaps for the
reason that the High Court heard the Writ Petition and
reserved the case for Judgment on 02.08.2018, but has
delivered it after four years i.e. on 07.04.2022.
7. It is necessary to mention that the High Court
will  have  to  necessarily  examine  the  contentions
raised by the parties as regards the legality and
validity of the auction sale, the subsistence of the
interim order at a time when the auction was conducted
and such other grounds that may be raised by the
parties before the High Court.
8. In view of above, we allow the appeal and set
aside the Judgment and Order passed by the High Court
and restore the writ petition to its original number.
9. In view of the fact that the auction sale was
conducted wayback in the year 2003, we request the
High Court to take up and dispose of the writ petition
expeditiously,  preferably  within  a  period  of  six
months from today.
10. The parties are directed to maintain status quo,
as on today, till the High Court disposes of the writ

petition.

3. Having perused the order(s) passed

appellants; and the High Court as well, has
committed an error by directing the Trial
Court to frame charges instead of remitting
the  matter  back  to  the  Trial  Court  to
consider the material in the charge sheet to
find out as to whether or not, there are
sufficient material for framing of charge
against the appellants.

the order dated 29.07.2024 passed by the
Trial Court and the impugned order dated
06.02.2026, passed by the High Court as well
and remit the matters back to the Trial
Court to hear the parties and decide the
issue of framing of charge afresh.

expressed any opinion on the merits of the
matters and the same shall be considered by
the  Trial  Court  basing  on  the  material
available in the charge sheet.

     UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
I.A. NO. 195478/2025
1. This matter has come up today to consider the plea of
the appellant (convict) for suspension of sentence of
life imprisonment and release on bail, pending the
final disposal of his criminal appeal before us, which
we have already admitted.
2. It is alleged that the deceased, son of complainant,
was assaulted by the appellant on the backside of his
neck with a Dau (concave shaped sharp cutting weapon),
which  resulted  in  his  instant  death.  During
investigation, it came to light that the eldest minor
daughter of the appellant was having an affair with the
deceased. That, on the date of incident (07.03.2017),
the appellant is alleged to have witnessed his minor
daughter being sexually exploited by the deceased,
Criminal Appeal  No.1950/2025                                      2

## Page 431

which  is  allegedly  stated  to  be  the  reason  for
committing the offence.
3. We take notice of the fact that the appellant was put
to trial for the offence punishable under Section 302
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, “the IPC”).
The Trial Court, relying on the corroborated eyewitness
evidence, held the appellant guilty of the alleged
crime and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for
life and pay fine of Rs.2,000/- (Rupees Two Thousand
only) in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for
six months in S.T.No.60/2017 arising out of G.R. Case
No.102 of 2012 corresponding to Rayagada P.S. Case
No.13/2017 of the Court of Sub Divisional Judicial
Magistrate (S.D.J.M.), Paralakhemundi.
4. Being dissatisfied with the confirmation of conviction
and sentence by the High Court, the appellant filed
this Criminal Appeal before us.
5. We take notice of the fact that the appellant is in
jail more than 9 years.
6. On a prima facie consideration, we are of the opinion
that the sentence imposed on the appellant can be
Criminal Appeal  No.1950/2025                                      3

## Page 432

suspended pending the final disposal of his criminal
appeal before this Court and the appellant released for
the time being. 
7. In view of the aforesaid, we suspend the substantive
order of sentence of life imprisonment imposed on the
appellant and order that the appellant be released on
bail forthwith, if not required in any other case,
subject to terms and conditions that the trial court
may deem fit to impose, pending the final disposal of
his appeal before this Court.
8. In the aforesaid, the I.A. No. 195478/2025 is allowed.
9. Notify the main appeal in due course.
(CHANDRESH)                                   (POOJA SHARMA)

O R D E R
1. Having heard the learned senior counsel appearing for the
parties at length, we are of the opinion that it would be
appropriate for the appellant, Unnati Fortune Industries Pvt.
Ltd., to make use of the liberty granted by the National
Company Law Appellate Tribunal 1, Principal Bench, New Delhi,
in  paragraph  7  of  the  impugned  order  dated  13.12.2024.
Thereby, it was left open to the appellant to take recourse to
legal  remedies  available  to  it  against  the  order  dated
19.01.2024.
2. We may note that the aforestated order dated 19.01.2024 was
passed by the Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority 2,
pursuant to the order dated 27.03.2023, passed by the National
Company Law Tribunal3, Principal Bench, New Delhi, in I.A. No.
1598/2023 in I.B. No.  452(PB)/2018. 
1  For short “NCLAT”
2  For short “ GNOIDA”
3  For short “NCLT”
1

## Page 434

3. We may also note that the aforestated order dated 27.03.2023
required the GNOIDA to consider the appellant’s representation
and dispose of the same within 60 days from the date of
receipt of a copy of the said order. 
4. Admittedly, the order that came to be passed by the GNOIDA was
well beyond the stipulated time, as it was dated 19.01.2024. 
5. In the meanwhile, the appellant had approached the NCLT, New
Delhi, by way of I.A. No. 4814/2023 reiterating its challenge
to the demands made by the GNOIDA on the ground that the
representation had not been considered till the date of the
filing of such application. The order dated 19.01.2024 came to
be passed by the GNOIDA during the pendency of the said I.A. 
6. While so, the NCLT dismissed the I.A. on the short ground that
the order dated 19.01.2024 had not been subjected to challenge
before it. 
7. This view was affirmed by the NCLAT in the appeal filed by the
appellant,  vide order dated 13.12.2024 passed in Company
Appeal (AT)(INS) No. 2216/2024. 
8. As already noted above, paragraph 7 of the impugned order
dated 13.12.2024 passed by the NCLAT records the liberty
granted to the appellant to take steps in relation to the
aforestated  order  dated  19.01.2024.  Reiterating  the
aforestated liberty, the present appeal is disposed of. 
9. However, the pendency of proceedings would not preclude the
appellant from remitting the rentals due and payable by it to
the GNOIDA for the period after completion of the corporate

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.10927-10929/2026

(SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) Diary No.35705/2023)
M/S TUF METALLURGICAL PVT. LTD.                    Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
GAURAV AGRAWAL & ORS.                              Respondent(s)
 O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. Application seeking deletion of proforma Respondent No.16 is
allowed from the array of parties.
3. Cause title be amended accordingly.
4. These appeals arise from three interim Orders dated 6-5-2022,
24-7-2023 and 24-8-2023 respectively in Company Appeal No.1 of 2022
passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh, by which the High Court
entertained  the  Writ  Applications  preferred  by  the  private
Respondents before us.
5. What we have been able to gather is that the appellant before
us was a financial creditor to the corporate debtor. Following a
default on repayment of loan, the appellant instituted insolvency
proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (for
short, “the IBC”) and the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process
was set in motion. The appellant, as a resolution applicant,
proposed a resolution plan before the Committee of Creditors.
6. A revised resolution plan was later submitted. This revised
plan was approved by the National Company Law Tribunal, Delhi vide

## Page 438

2
Order dated 5th November, 2019. This Order, passed by the NCLT, was
made a subject matter of challenge before the High Court. 
7. Having heard the learned council appearing for the parties,
and having gone through the materials on record, we are of the view
that  the  High  Court  ought  not  to  have  exercised  its  writ
jurisdiction against the Order passed by the NCLT. Against any
Order passed by the NCLT, if a party is aggrieved, the party has to
go before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal
Bench, Delhi. There was no good reason for the High Court to
entertain the Writ Applications. 
8. On this short ground alone, we set aside all the three Orders
impugned before us. 
9. We leave it for the respondents to avail appropriate legal
remedy before the appropriate forum in accordance with law insofar
as their other grievances are concerned, 
10. We clarify that we have otherwise not expressed any opinion on
merits of the case.
11. With the aforesaid, the appeals stand disposed of.
12. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

      UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the petitioner(s) and learned Senior counsel appearing
for the respondent(s).
2. On the main issue, law is quite settled and has been
reiterated by this Court in several judgments with the
last one being that of a larger Bench in  Union  of
India vs. Ramesh  Ram and Ors. reported in (2010) 7 SCC
234. In  such  view  of  the  matter,  there  is  no
difficulty in holding that a person who is otherwise
eligible under the reserved category and has been
fitted into the open category, is entitled to a better
post under the reserved category as against a person
who has secured lesser marks than him in the reserved
category.
3. However, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
respondent(s) submits that the petitioner(s) before us
have in fact availed a relaxation. We do not find any
material to substantiate the same.
4. Learned counsel appearing for the State and for the
Jharkhand Public Service Commission seek six weeks’
time to file an affidavit in this regard.
5. The  incidental  issue  is  on  the  position  of  the
3

## Page 460

unreserved  candidates  in  the  event  of  a  reserved
candidate who has migrated to the unreserved category,
being sent back to a reserved post of his choice.
6. List on 25.08.2026.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioners are the plaintiffs in a suit for specific
performance, who are aggrieved with the denial of injunction, by
the trial court and also by the High Court in appeal, which orders
are impugned herein.
2. We have heard Sri Gopal Subramanium, learned Senior Counsel
appearing for the petitioners and Sri Mukul Rohatgi, learned Senior
Counsel appearing for the respondents.
3. On facts, suffice it to notice that the suit for specific
performance was opposed on the contention that the agreement of
sale was only to secure a loan advanced. The trial court found on
examination of the facts coming out from the records that there was
in fact an arrangement between the petitioners and the respondents.
The respondents were also aware of the construction being carried
out in the property, after obtaining sanctions and permissions from
the local authority. Text of WhatsApp messages produced also
indicated money transactions in aid of the construction and not as
an advance in pursuance of an agreement to sell. The trial court
found suppression on the part of the plaintiffs and prayer for
interim injunction.
4. The High Court concurred with the order of the trial court and
found that essentially the question is as to whether the agreement
was one intended for sale of the property or a joint venture.
2

## Page 483

However, the suppression found by the trial court as against the
plaintiffs  was  concurred  with  and  the  injunction  prayer  was
declined. The order of status quo granted by the trial court was
extended, limited to the 50% saleable area, wherein the defendants
were directed not to create any third party interest for four weeks
only to enable the petitioners to approach this Court.
5. We were not inclined to interfere with the order passed by the
trial court and affirmed by the High Court. Sri Gopal Subramanium,
then prayed that the interim order, as granted by the High Court
may be made absolute till the disposal of the suit. The said
contention was raised on the ground that even if the defense is
accepted and there is no claim for specific performance, still the
petitioners would be entitled to 50% of the saleable area.
6. Sri  Mukul  Rohatgi,  however,  opposed  the  said  claim  and
asserted that there was not even a joint venture and it was just a
financial transaction and there cannot even be a claim of right to
50% of the saleable area.
7. Admittedly, the development work is going on, as carried out
by the defendants, who are the owners of the property. The
development is also intended at creating third party rights, and in
such circumstances, we do not think there is a reason to impair the
development activity or prohibit the owners of the property from
creating third party interests, especially since that is the very
intention of carrying out the development of the land. We would
also not want the unsuspecting third parties inducted therein to
suffer on account of the suit agitated before the trial court
between the petitioners and the respondents.
3

## Page 484

8. On the above reasoning, we confirm the order passed by the
trial court, rejecting the injunction sought for. We make it clear
that if at all the petitioners are found to have a claim against
the property, either for specific performance or a share in the
saleable area, the same can be made good by the computation of
damages by the trial court. This would enable the project to go on
and protect the innocent purchasers if third party rights are
created and also enable a fair adjudication of the dispute between
the parties in the suit.
9. With the above observations, the special leave petition stands
disposed of, leaving open all contentions of the parties to be
agitated in the suit, untramelled by any observation made by the
High Court and this Court.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

CIVIL APPEAL No. 639 OF 2017
UNION OF INDIA AND ORS.                                    APPELLANTS
                                VERSUS
    JAGDISH KUMAR MADHAJI AND ORS.                    RESPONDENTS
   
O R D E R
1. Union of India and two officers of the Western Railway are in appeal, by
special leave granted on 10th January, 2017, challenging the judgment and order
dated 20th March, 2013 of a Division Bench of the High Court of Gujarat at
Ahmedabad, whereby the Special Civil Application 1 instituted by the first
respondent was allowed with the following directions:
“11. In the result, the petition succeeds. Judgment and order of
the Hon’ble Central Administrative Tribunal is quashed and set aside.
The petitioners be given all consequential benefits as if the impugned
order is not passed. Taking into consideration the fact that the
petitioners are from lower strata of society and must be passing
through  very  harsh  days,  it  is  expected  that  the  Railway
Administration will reinstate them as early as possible, but not later
than six weeks from today. The petition is allowed in the aforesaid
terms. Rule is made absolute. No order as to cost.”
2. It is significant to note that the Special Civil Application was directed
against an order dated 7 th October, 2004 passed by the Central Administrative
1  No.14645 of 2004

## Page 498

2
Tribunal, Ahmedabad Bench, Ahmedabad2 dismissing the original application3 of

3. Incidentally, the said judgment dated 7 th October, 2004 also dismissed
original applications4 of the second to sixth respondents. However, the said
respondents had not independently challenged the dismissal of their original
applications before the High Court; instead, they have applied for impleadment
in the writ petition of the first respondent which was allowed and they were
treated as co-petitioners.
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the appellants as well as

5. It is not in dispute that pursuant to the impugned order dated 20 th March,

issuing notice on the special leave petition, granted interim stay of the
operation of the impugned judgment and order by its order dated 13 th
September, 2013.  
6. A subsequent order dated 11 th November, 2013 recorded the fact of
reinstatement of the respondents in service but restrained payment of back
wages until further orders.
7. The controversy arose because of dismissal of the respondents following
disciplinary proceedings. Though the Tribunal held against the respondents, the
High Court found the proceedings to be utterly flawed and, thus, allowed the
writ petition.
8. Since all the respondents, upon reinstatement, were allowed to discharge
services till their respective dates of retirement on superannuation and also

Counsel for the petitioner and  Mr. Abhishek Saket,

## Page 533

2
2. The  present  petition  calls  in  question  the
correctness of the judgment/order dated 13-04-2026 in
CRMBA No. 39929/2025 passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Allahabad. By the said judgment/order,
the High Court has denied the benefit of bail pending
trial, to the petitioner in connection with FIR/Crime
No.96/2023  registered  with  Majhola  Police  Station,
District Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh,  for the offences
punishable under Section s 498-A/304-B of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860. 
3. We have perused the records. The petitioner has
already put in custody for three years and six months
approximately.
4. It is not disputed that pursuant to a petition
filed by the petitioner under Section 482 of the Code
of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the trial has been stayed
by the High Court on 27.08.2025.
5. Considering the period already undergone by the
petitioner and the likelihood the trial taking some
time to conclude as also keeping in mind the overall
facts and circumstances of the case, we are inclined to
enlarge the petitioner on bail pending trial.
6. Accordingly, we direct that petitioner shall be
enlarged on bail subject to the satisfaction of the
concerned Trial Court in connection with the aforesaid
FIR and for the offences mentioned hereinabove.
7. At this stage, learned counsel for the State

## Page 534

3
submits that the petitioner has filed an application
under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha
Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNSS’) bearing No.32237/2025
(page 157 of the paper books) seeking quashment of
proceedings is enjoying the benefit of interim orders.
Learned counsel for the State submits that the quash
petition should be decided early so that depending on
the outcome, parties can adjust their affairs.
8. We are of the opinion, that considering the
nature of the aforesaid application under Section 528
of BNSS No.32237/2025 should be heard at an early date.
The High Court make an endevour to dispose of the quash
petition within a period of six months from today.
9. Let  a  copy  of  this  order  be  sent  to  the
Registrar General of the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad with a direction to place the same before
Hon’ble Chief Justice of the High Court of Judicature
at Allahabad, for appropriate directions.
10. With the above observations, the Special Leave
Petition is disposed of.
11. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also
stand disposed of.

1. The appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated
16th December, 2015 1 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay,
Nagpur Bench, Nagpur2.
2. The Caste Scrutiny Committee invalidated the respondent’s
caste claim. His prayer for protection of his service was allowed by
a Division Bench of the High Court placing reliance on the decision
of this Court in Kavita Solunke v. State of Maharashtra3 and a
Full Bench decision of the High Court in  Arun s/o Vishwanath
Sonone v. State of Maharashtra4. 
3. A  Bench  of  three  Judges  of  this  Court  in  Chairman and
Managing  Director,  Food  Corporation  of  India  &  Ors.  v.
Jagdish Balaram Bahira & Ors.5 has over-ruled Kavita Solunke
(supra) as well as Arun Sonone (supra).
1 impugned judgment
2 High Court
3 (2012) 8 SCC 430
4 2015 (1) Mh. L.J. 457
5 (2017) 8 SCC 670
1

## Page 536

4. Therefore, the basis for grant of relief to the respondent by
the  High  Court  ceases  to  survive.  We  set  aside  the  impugned
judgment and allow the civil appeal.
5. At this stage, we are informed that a special leave petition
challenging the judgment in Arun Sonone (supra) is still pending.
We grant liberty to the respondent to approach this Court for recall
of this order, should a larger Bench of this Court overrule Jagdish
Balaram Bahira (supra) and restore the law laid down in Kavita
Solunke (supra).
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

learned senior counsel appearing for the respondents.
2. After hearing the matter for some time, we put it
to the learned counsel for the parties that it was
eminently a fit case where an amicable solution to put a
quietus to all the pending disputes between the parties
arising out of a consent decree, should be explored
through the process of mediation.  Both the parties, on
instructions,  have  favourably  responded  to  the
suggestion,  without  prejudice  to  their  rights  and
contentions.
3. We also put it to learned senior counsel for the
petitioners that, as a pre-requisite, unconditionally the
amount  of  Rs.12,00,00,000/-  (Rupees  twelve  crores)
deposited in this Court, pursuant to the order of this
Court dated 15 th October, 2025 would be released to the
two  respondents,  with  accrued  interest,  in  equal
proportions.
4. We  direct  that  the  amount  of  Rs.12,00,00,000/-
(Rupees twelve crores) with accrued interest lying in
this Court will be unconditionally released to the two
respondents equally.
5. The  Registry  shall  release  the  amount  of
Rs.12,00,00,000/- (Rupees twelve crores) with accrued
interest to the respondents after due verification of
their identity.

Justice  Sanjay  Vijaykumar  Gangapurwala,  former  Chief

Mediator.  The fee and other terms of the mediation shall
be fixed in consultation with the learned Mediator.

Sanjay Vijaykumar Gangapurwala, former Chief Justice of
the Madras High Court.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  petitioner before  this Court  has filed  the
present petition, being aggrieved by the impugned order
dated 08.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad in Criminal Misc. Anticipatory Bail Application
No. 3864/2026, rejecting the prayer for anticipatory bail
in  connection  with  FIR/Crime  Case  No.  427  of  2024,
registered at Police Station Sigra, District Varanasi,
Uttar Pradesh, for the offences punishable under Sections
108, 115(2), 351(2) and 352 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
2. This Court, vide order dated 01.07.2026, granted
interim protection to the petitioner in the matter.
3. Reply has been filed in the matter and learned
counsel for the respondent-State has vehemently opposed the
prayer for grant of anticipatory bail.
4. The petitioner, who is the wife, has been charged
for an offences under Sections 108, 115(2), 351(2) and 352
of the BNS.
5. Learned counsel for the petitioner has argued before
this Court that there is no proximity between the suicide
and the alleged allegations levelled against the wife
dragging the husband to commit suicide. The prayer for
grant of bail has been vehemently opposed by the learned
2

## Page 594

counsel for the respondent-State as well as learned counsel
for the respondent No.2. 
6. This Court after hearing learned counsel for the
parties and keeping in view the grounds raised by the
petitioner and also that the petitioner has co-operated
with the investigation, is of the opinion that the interim
order dated 01.07.2026 deserves to be made absolute.
7. Accordingly, interim order dated 01.07.2026 is made
absolute subject to the condition that petitioner shall
continue to co-operate with the investigation and shall
report  as  and  when  called  upon  to  do  so  by  the
Investigating Authority.
8. The Special Leave Petition is accordingly disposed
of in the above terms.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

1. We  have  heard  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
petitioner. The respondents are represented by learned

2. Even without issuance of notice, we have heard the
learned senior counsel and learned counsel for the
respective parties.
3. We direct the matter to be referred to the Supreme
Court Mediation Centre.
4. The  parties,  namely,  the  petitioner  and  the  third
respondent-husband are directed to appear in-person
before the Supreme Court Mediation Centre on 02.09.2026
at 11.30 A.M.
5. We request that an experienced Mediator be appointed so
as to enable the parties to resolve their differences
amicably.
6. The third respondent shall keep the minor child present
before the Supreme Court Mediation Centre on the said
date so as to enable the petitioner to interact with
the child.
7. The Report of the learned Mediator shall be placed on
record.
8. List the matter immediately thereafter.
9. In the meanwhile, the petitioner is at liberty to
interact with the child through video conferencing

                             O R D E R
SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) Nos.1275-1276/2020
1. Learned counsel appearing for the parties have drawn this Court’s
attention to the order dated 15 th February, 2024 wherein it has been
recorded that the respondent no.6 has died.
2. They jointly submit that there are only three respondents in the
special leave petition and it is the petitioner viz. Ramesh who has passed
away on 26th September, 2023.
3. Applications have been filed by the heirs/legal representatives of
deceased-petitioner  viz.  Ramesh  seeking  substitution  (I.A.
No.66853/2024),  setting  aside  abatement  (I.A.  No.66856/2024)  and
condonation of delay in filing the application (I.A. No.66857/2024) for
setting aside abatement.
4. Having heard learned counsel for the petitioner and learned counsel
appearing for the respondents 2 & 3, the applications are allowed.
5. The heirs//legal representatives, as mentioned in paragraph no.5 of
the application (I.A. No.66853/2024), be brought on record as substituted
petitioners.
6. However, this order is subject to just exceptions, if any, that may be
taken at the time of final hearing by the non-appearing respondents.
7. Amended memo of parties be filed within two weeks from date.
8. The special leave petitions may be re-listed thereafter before an
appropriate bench.

1. Learned counsel for the appellant has placed reliance on the decision of
this Court in Nandkishore Shravan Ahirrao Vs. Kosan Industries Private
Limited1 to contend that though back wages were denied to the appellant, he
was entitled to claim continuity in service having been reinstated pursuant to
the award dated 25th November, 1988 of the Labour Court, Hubli2.
2. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State of Karnataka submits
that the High Court of Karnataka, Dharwad Bench3 was right in refusing relief to
the appellant on the ground of res  judicata  and/or analogous principles. The
Labour Court having refused the prayer for back wages, it stands to reason that
1 (2021) 14 SCC 781
2 Labour Court
3 High Court

the Labour Court did not intend to grant benefit of continuity in service to the
appellant.
3. We require the respondent-State of Karnataka to place before this Court
the statement of claim lodged by the appellant before the Labour Court, the
written statement thereto of the State as well as copies of the writ petition and
the intra-court appeal by filing an application for placing on record additional
documents within three weeks from date.
4. Re-list the civil appeal thereafter.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Order dated 07 th October, 2025 on a writ petition 1 and order dated 22 nd
June, 2026 on a contempt petition passed by separate Division Benches of the
High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Circuit Bench at Kolhapur 2, are under
challenge in these special leave petitions.
2. Challenge to the order dated 07 th October, 2025 is delayed by 181 days.
There is also refiling delay of 5 days.
3. We have looked into the application for condonation of delay and find that
1 WP No.4456 of 2025
2 High Court
1

## Page 857

scanty reasons have been provided in support of the prayer for condonation. Mr.
Mehta, learned senior counsel for the respondents submits that no case for
condonation having been set up, the special leave petition challenging the order
dated 07th October, 2025 ought to be dismissed as time-barred.
4. Having heard the parties, we allow the prayer for condonation of delay,
subject to payment of cost of Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees one lakh) only to the
respondents by the next date of hearing.
5. Insofar as the merits are concerned, we are prima facie satisfied that the
High Court may not have been right in disposing of the writ petition on 07 th
October, 2025 without looking into the aspect of compliance with Section 3E of
the National Highways Act, 1956.
6. Issue notice.
7. Mr. Ashok Mathur, learned counsel accepts notice on behalf of respondent
no.1. Service of formal notice, thus, stands dispensed with.
8. There shall be stay of proceedings for contempt before the High Court.
9. Since we are informed by learned counsel for the petitioner that the
interest component in terms of the orders dated 7 th October, 2025 and the
orders on the contempt petition have been deposited with the Registrar General
of the High Court, we await counter affidavit from the side of the respondents.
10. Counter-affidavit may be filed by two weeks. Rejoinder thereto, if any,
may be filed by a week thereafter.
11. Liberty is granted to the advocate-on-record for the petitioner to file the
correct version of the award.
12. Re-list the special leave petitions after four weeks.

3. Accordingly, the Special Leave Petition stands dismissed.
4. However, if the petitioner appears before the Court below and
seeks bail, the same shall be considered on its own merits without
being prejudiced by the present order.
5. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

We have heard Shri  Siddhartha Dave,  learned senior  
counsel for the petitioner,  learned standing counsel for  
respondent no.1/State and learned senior counsel appearing for
respondent no.2/informant extensively.
Contd..

## Page 1095

- 2 -
We have also perused the material on record. 
We do not find this to be a case where any interference 
is called for vis-a-vis the impugned order so as to consider 
the petitioner’s case for bail. 
The Special Leave Petition is hence dismissed.
However, we notice that the petitioner has been in jail 
since  21/22.03.2023 and the charges were framed only on  
22.05.2026.  We are informed that there are as many as 83 
witnesses and possibly the number of witnesses may be tailored
down but the examination of witnesses is yet to commence. 
In the circumstances, we direct the concerned Sessions 
Court to ensure that the parties as well as their respective 
counsel cooperate for conclusion of the trial as expeditiously
as possible.
We also reserve liberty to the petitioner herein to seek 
bail once the material witnesses are examined by making an 
application before the Trial Court.
Pending application(s) shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have been informed that the Ministry of Environment and
Wildlife has issued mandatory guidelines to ensure seamless and
unobstructed elephant corridor passing through different States.
However, owing to certain local factors, the elephant corridors
have been impeded/blocked/obstructed.
2. We, therefore, direct the Ministry concerned in the Union of
India to conduct a fresh survey and submit a comprehensive report,
including the necessary steps taken by them to prevent such
obstructions. The status report shall also indicate steps taken to
prohibit the use of fireballs,  mashaals, or any other coercive
measure to divert the natural movement of the elephants. A specific
ban on ‘Hulla Parties’, etc. would also be required in this regard,
and this Court shall be apprised about the action taken on the same
through the aforesaid status report.
3. Post the matters for further consideration on 14.10.2026.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

## Page 1235

                             O R D E R
1.  The Petitioners who are direct recruits to the post of Deputy
Collectors and who came to be appointed on 09.12.2026 and who are not
parties to the impugned order or questioning the same on the ground that the
review DPC ordered under the impugned order may disturb their seniority and
the service rights accrued to them. If the review DPC is held retrospectively. At
the outset, it requires to be noticed that the apprehension of the petitioners are
premature and they are attempting to put the cart before the horse. In fact,
there is no cause of action for the present petition at all. Only in the event of
the promotees being granted retrospective promotion after review DPC being
held and as a consequence thereof the petitioners’ seniority is being disturbed,
they would get a cause of action to challenge the same and as such without
expressing any opinion in that regard and reserving liberty to challenge such
order if any, we reject the prayer for granting leave to file the Special Leave
Petition and consequently reject the petition also.
2. We have not expressed any opinion on merits of the case.
3. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
We fail to understand as to how the petitioner, who has
always been prevaricating with his request for allotment of a 
flat has now filed this special leave petition. Although, the
RERA/Tribunal granted relief to the petitioner herein and the
said relief has been sustained by the High Court, we  find
that filing of this special leave petition is an abuse of the
process of law and of this Court. 
Further, there  is  a delay of 244 days in filing the
special  leave  petition. 
contd..

The special leave petition is dismissed both on the 
ground of delay as well as on merits.
However, we refrain from imposing costs in the  
matter.

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE R. MAHADEVAN
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. N Venkataraman, A.S.G.

                   Mr. Brijesh Yadav, Adv.                         
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
There  is  a gross  delay of 902 days in filing the
special leave petition. The reasons assigned for seeking 
condonation  of  delay  are  neither  satisfactory  nor  
sufficient in law to condone the same. Hence, the  
application seeking condonation of delay is dismissed. 
Further, we find that the issues which are raised in 
the special leave petition are  covered  by the judgment
of this Court in Civil  Appeal  No. 6580  of 2021  
(Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-3 v/s. 
contd..

## Page 1283

- 2 -
 Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.) rendered on 24.04.2023. In the
circumstances,  the  special  leave  petition  is  also  
dismissed in terms of the said judgment on merits.
We fail to understand  as  to  how  the  
petitioner/Department  has  filed  this  special  leave  
petition with 902 days delay when even according to the 
Department  the  matter  is  covered  by  an  earlier  
judgment of this Court in Civil  Appeal  No. 6580  of 
2021 (Principal Commissioner of  Income  Tax,  
Central-3 v/s. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.) rendered on 
24.04.2023.  This is an instance of burdening this  
Court with an unnecessary special leave petition and  
adding to the pendency. 
Pending application(s) shall stand disposed of.
